purpose: Vemurafenib is used to treat a type of skin cancer called melanoma that has spread to other parts of the body or cannot be removed by surgery. It is specifically for patients whose cancer has a certain gene change called a BRAF V600 mutation. Your doctor will test your tumor to make sure this medicine is right for you.
how_it_works: Inside some cancer cells, there is a faulty protein made by a mutated BRAF gene that tells the cancer to keep growing out of control. Vemurafenib works like a targeted 'off switch' that blocks this faulty protein, slowing down or stopping the cancer from growing. Because it targets a specific change in cancer cells, it works differently from traditional chemotherapy.
common_side_effects: Very common side effects include skin rash, joint pain, hair loss, feeling tired or weak, nausea, itching, and increased sensitivity to sunlight (your skin can burn much more easily). Some patients also develop new non-cancerous skin growths like warts or a mild type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma, which your doctor will monitor closely.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious heart rhythm problems, severe skin reactions, liver problems, and eye inflammation. Because your skin becomes very sensitive to sunlight, you must use strong sunscreen, wear protective clothing, and avoid sun exposure while taking this drug. Tell your doctor right away if you notice unusual skin changes, yellowing of your eyes or skin, vision changes, or irregular heartbeat. This medication can also harm an unborn baby, so effective birth control is very important during treatment.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 960 mg (four 240 mg tablets) taken by mouth twice a day, roughly every 12 hours. It is best taken consistently with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time. Swallow the tablets whole and do not crush or chew them. If you miss a dose, skip it if your next dose is within 4 hours — never double up.
